title: The future is sweet: exploiting sugar allocation and use for cotton breeding
content: It is only natural for parents to worry about their children and make sure that they grow strong and healthy, ready to tackle any challenges they encounter. In their own way, plants also have strategies to ensure that their offspring grow vigorously. In the process, they must carefully allocate their resources among their successors, providing enough material for seeds to form and mature. Over years of evolution, this has led to a series of source-sink relationships, whereby nutrients are transported from the mother plant's tissues toward developing fruits (Fig. 1) (Braun et al. 2014). For crops, however, the interests of the mother plant do not always align with those of the agronomist. Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) is grown worldwide for its oil- and protein-rich seeds and, importantly, its fibers. Historically, breeders have favored varieties with higher fiber yield and quality. Directing more resources to fibers sometimes comes at the cost of fewer nutrients allocated to seeds and thus a loss in seed yield.
